2-3.indicator_name:
• Proportion of children and young people achieving a minimum proficiency level in reading and mathematics
  • Proportion of youth and adults with information and communications technology skills (ICT)
2-3.area_description:
Being educated supports informed participation in civic life and strengthens people’s sense of autonomy and dignity. At the same time, education and lifelong learning programmes provide the skills and capabilities required to adapt to changing labour markets, innovate and make forward-looking choices. Low educational attainment is associated with limited opportunities, lower quality of life and vulnerability to exclusion. Education also generates public benefits, contributes to better outcomes across generations, and supports broader social and economic development.
Source: "Counting What Counts: A Compass of Progress for People and Planet". Report of the Secretary-General`s Independent High-Level Expert Group on Beyond GDP.
2-3.info:
To assess competences at the end of primary education, the results of the Progress in International Reading Literacy Study (PIRLS) and the Trends in International Mathematics and Science Study (TIMSS), conducted by the International Association for the Evaluation of Educational Achievement (IAE), are used. The ‘Low’ proficiency level is set as the minimum standard.

The assessment of competences at the end of lower secondary education is based on the results of the Programme for International Student Assessment (PISA) conducted by the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD). In PISA, proficiency level 2 is considered the minimum standard.

2-8.indicator_name:
• Annual mean levels of fine particulate matter in cities
  • Proportion of population using safely managed drinking water services
2-8.area_description:
Environmental quality is central to both present and future well-being. Environmental degradation directly affects health, livelihoods and life satisfaction, while climate-related risks threaten lives and economic security.
Source: "Counting What Counts: A Compass of Progress for People and Planet". Report of the Secretary-General`s Independent High-Level Expert Group on Beyond GDP.
2-8.info:
• Annual mean levels of fine particulate matter are determined using a combination of model calculations and measurement data provided by the Federal Environment Agency (UBA) and the Länder. For this indicator, only data from background monitoring stations in urban and rural areas that are not directly influenced by local emission sources such as traffic or industrial plants are used. This provides as representative a picture as possible of large-scale particulate matter pollution, without individual local pollution hotspots influencing the result.
  • The legal framework for water supply in Germany is governed at federal level by the Water Resources Act (WHG) and at state level by the respective water laws of the federal states. Water supply is a public service and is generally provided by local authorities. The obligation to connect to and use the public water supply serves to ensure a reliable supply of drinking water to the population and to prevent or restrict the private use of groundwater. Over 99% of the population in Germany is connected to centralised drinking water distribution networks.

3-3.national_indicator_available: At-risk-of-poverty rate at national poverty line
3-3.indicator_name: Poverty headcount ratio at societal poverty line (fixed at a baseline)
3-3.area_description: Poverty limits people’s ability to meet their basic needs and lead self-determined lives. It affects not only income, but can also manifest itself in limited access to housing, education, healthcare and social participation. Examining poverty reveals whether economic and social progress is reaching all sections of the population, thereby contributing to a more comprehensive assessment of quality of life and prosperity.
3-3.differences: The data shown represents the proportion of the population living below the national, country-specific poverty line. According to the EU Convention, this is set at 60 percent of the median net equivalent income of the country in question. The societal poverty line’ mentioned in the indicator, with a fixed baseline, refers to a World Bank definition, according to which the poverty line is stated in purchasing power adjusted 2021 U.S. dollars and is defined as $1.30 + 0.5 * median income, but is set at a minimum level of $3.00 where the median income is very low.
3-3.source_organisation_1: Federal Statistical Office (Destatis)
3-3.source_organisation_2: Statistical office of the European Union (Eurostat)
3-3.source_url_text_2: EU-SILC survey: At-risk-of-poverty rate: Eurostat table [ilc_li02]
3-3.data_footnotes:
• Eurostat definition: The national poverty line is a benchmark for measuring country-specific poverty in terms of economic and social circumstances. According to the EU Convention, the 60 % of the median net equivalent income is the at-risk-of-poverty threshold.
  • Due to methodological changes resulting from the integration of EU-SILC into the Microcensus in the 2020 survey year, the results from 2020 onwards are only comparable with previous years to a limited extent (break in the time series).

1-1.area_description:
The notion of peace encompasses both the absence of violence and the assurance of physical security, as well as a broader, positive conception that includes the structural conditions that enable societies, through their norms and institutions, to manage conflict, foster cooperation and sustain well-being over time. As Nelson Mandela acknowledged, “[p]eace is not just the absence of conflict; peace is the creation of an environment where all can flourish, regardless of race, colour, creed, religion, gender, class, caste or any other social markers of difference”.
Source: "Counting What Counts: A Compass of Progress for People and Planet". Report of the Secretary-General`s Independent High-Level Expert Group on Beyond GDP.

1-2.area_description:
Human rights, as enshrined in the Universal Declaration of Human Rights and the wider body of international human rights law, which recognize that “all human rights are universal, indivisible, and interdependent and interrelated”. This includes civic and political rights as well as economic, social and cultural rights. Progress and human rights are intertwined, and one can scarcely exist without the other. At the same time, we recognize the progressive realization approach to human rights, whereby consideration is given to the financial and other resources available to a government when assessing its compliance with its obligations with respect to civil, social and economic rights.

2-1.indicator_name:
• Household disposable income per capita
  • Composite rate of labour underutilization
  • Proportion of time spent on unpaid domestic and care work
2-1.area_description:
While well-being is not determined by income alone, sufficient material resources are a necessary condition for people to exercise choice and agency in their lives. Without adequate means, individuals and families are constrained to meeting day-to-day needs. Persistent material deprivation undermines people’s ability to plan, invest in their future, and participate in society fully. Beyond the monetary benefits of employment, work also provides a sense of dignity and self-realization.
Source: "Counting What Counts: A Compass of Progress for People and Planet". Report of the Secretary-General`s Independent High-Level Expert Group on Beyond GDP.
2-1.info:
The Composite rate of labour underutilization (LU4) indicates the proportion of the extended labour force accounted for by the unemployed, those who are underemployed in terms of hours worked, and the potential labour force. It therefore takes into account not only unemployment but also the underutilisation of the labour supply by people who would like to work longer hours and are available to do so, as well as by people who are outside the labour force but have a need for gainful employment.

The rate is calculated as a proportion of the extended labour force:
LU4 = (unemployed + time-related underemployed + potential labour force) / (labour force + potential labour force) × 100.

3-2.area_description: Income influences people’s ability to meet their basic needs and participate in society. Significant disparities in disposable income can lead to unequal life chances and undermine social participation, trust and social cohesion. Examining income inequality therefore complements average measures of economic prosperity by addressing the question of how economic resources are distributed amongst the population.
3-2.info:
The Gini coefficient is a measure of relative inequality, taking values between zero and one. Under conditions of perfect equality, it equals zero; under conditions of maximum inequality, it reaches one. In the context of income distribution, a Gini coefficient of one means that all income accrues to a single individual. The lower the value, the more evenly income is distributed.

The equivalised income is a needs-adjusted income derived from the total household income and the number and age of household members. Using an equivalence scale, incomes are weighted according to household size and composition. This adjustment ensures that the incomes of individuals from households of different sizes are comparable, as larger households benefit from economies of scale – for example, through the shared use of living space or household appliances.
The market equivalised income denotes income before deduction of taxes and social contributions and without taking social transfers into account.

2-5.area_description:
This domain captures how people perceive and experience their lives, which influences their behaviour, aspirations and investment in the future. The gap between people’s perceptions and many objective indicators points to the value of measuring people’s subjective experience to capture elements that are not otherwise observed.
Source: "Counting What Counts: A Compass of Progress for People and Planet". Report of the Secretary-General`s Independent High-Level Expert Group on Beyond GDP.

2-7.indicator_name: Proportion of population satisfied with their last experience of public services
2-7.area_description:
Quality of institutions is essential to current well-being, equity and inclusiveness, and sustainability. Effective institutions underpin the delivery of public services, the protection of rights and the functioning of markets. They shape whether policies are implemented fairly and whether citizens can trust public systems. Weak institutions are consistently associated with poor economic performance, inequality and instability.
Source: "Counting What Counts: A Compass of Progress for People and Planet". Report of the Secretary-General`s Independent High-Level Expert Group on Beyond GDP.
2-7.source_organisation_1: Federal Statistical Office (Destatis)
2-7.data_footnotes:
• The data is based on a special evaluation and is not publicly available.
  • The data relates to experiences with public services over the last 24 months.
  • Data is only available from 2015.
2-7.data_last_update: Last updated on 2024/10/04. Data for further reporting periods will be added as soon as it becomes available.

4-2.indicator_name:
• Share of youth not in education, employment or training (NEET)
  • Potential years of life lost (PYLL), all causes
4-2.area_description: People’s knowledge, skills and health are essential resources for social and economic development. Investment in education, skills and health broadens individuals’ opportunities whilst also strengthening a society’s capacity for innovation and adaptability. Human capital is therefore a key foundation for long-term prosperity and for the ability to overcome future social and economic challenges.
4-2.info: „Potential Years of Life Lost“ (PYLL) is a summary indicator of premature mortality. It allows deaths in younger age groups, which are generally regarded as preventable, to be weighted. To calculate PYLL, deaths in each age group are totalled and weighted by the number of years of life remaining up to a specified age limit.

1-3.indicator_name:
• Total greenhouse gas emissions and greenhouse gas emissions per capita
  • Biodiversity intactness index
1-3.area_description:
Respect for the planet, including for planetary boundaries. Planetary boundaries are scientifically identified environmental limits within which humanity can safely operate on Earth. Once these boundaries are crossed, there is a high risk of irreparable damage to the planet and, by extension, major impacts on the well-being of its people.
Source: "Counting What Counts: A Compass of Progress for People and Planet". Report of the Secretary-General`s Independent High-Level Expert Group on Beyond GDP.
1-3.info:
The Biodiversity Index tracks trends in species diversity and landscape quality, using the populations of selected bird species as an example. It comprises 41 bird species that are representative of the most important landscape and habitat types in Germany. Ten species are included for each of the sub-indicators Forests, Settlements and Inland waters, and eleven species for Agricultural land. The sub-indicator for coasts and seas, which also comprises ten bird species, is presented as a supplementary measure, as its trends are particularly influenced by specific conservation measures.

For each sub-indicator, the arithmetic mean of the target achievement for the respective ten or eleven species considered is calculated. The overall indicator is calculated as the weighted sum of the sub-indicators. The weighting factors correspond to the area shares of the respective main habitat or landscape types: agricultural land 49%, forests 29%, settlements 13% and inland waters 9%.
